**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Paper 2: Section A - Composition; Section B - Prescribed Texts; Section C - Creative Writing. Duration: two hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised answer will earn you little or no marks.

**SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: define electoral fraud and say why it matters.
2. Forms of fraud: before, during and after polling day; vote buying and intimidation.
3. Causes: hunger for power, weak institutions, poverty, impunity.
4. Effects: lack of legitimacy, apathy, violence, loss of trust abroad.
5. Remedies, then a short conclusion.

**Model essay (544 words)**

Elections are the peaceful way in which citizens hand power to those they trust, but when the process is poisoned by fraud, the ballot box becomes a theatre in which the result is written before the first vote is cast. Electoral fraud, the deliberate manipulation of the voting process in order to change its outcome, is one of the most corrosive diseases of modern democracy, and many young nations continue to suffer from it.

Fraud takes many forms. Before polling day, voters' registers may be padded with the names of the dead and of people who do not exist, while genuine voters are quietly struck off. On the day itself, ballot boxes may be stuffed, the same person may vote several times, and the agents of one party may be chased from the polling stations. Afterwards, results may be altered in the counting room or announced without any connection to the figures signed at the polling stations. Less visible, but no less harmful, are the buying of votes with bags of rice and a few banknotes and the intimidation of voters who are warned of what will happen if they choose the wrong candidate.

Why does fraud persist? The first cause is the hunger for power: where public office is the quickest road to wealth, losing an election seems a catastrophe that must be avoided at any cost. Secondly, weak institutions, especially electoral bodies and courts that depend on the government they should supervise, offer cheats a safe harbour. Thirdly, poverty makes voters easy prey, since a hungry citizen will sell tomorrow for a meal today. Finally, impunity encourages repetition, since nobody who rigs an election is ever punished.

The consequences are grave. A leader who comes to power through fraud lacks legitimacy and often governs for his own circle rather than for the people. Citizens lose faith and stay at home on polling day, which makes the next fraud even easier. Frustration builds up, and when peaceful protest is ignored, it sometimes explodes into violence that destroys lives and property, as the history of several countries has shown. Investors and development partners also hesitate to trust a state whose government cannot prove that it was freely chosen.

Fortunately, the disease can be treated. Electoral commissions must be truly independent, with members chosen by consensus and protected from dismissal. Voters' registers should be public, regularly cleaned and, where possible, supported by biometric technology, while results should be posted at every polling station so that anyone can compare them with the final tally. The presence of party agents, local observers and the press at each stage discourages cheating. Courts must be able to cancel tainted results and to punish those who falsify them, whoever they are. Above all, civic education must teach citizens that their vote is not for sale and that the secret ballot is their strongest protection.

In conclusion, an election without integrity is a ceremony without meaning. A nation that wants peace, development and respect must ensure that its leaders are the real choice of its people. That demands vigilance from institutions, courage from judges and journalists, and honesty from every citizen who holds a ballot paper. Only then will the voice of the people be heard exactly as it was spoken.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A clear treatment of the topic (forms, causes, effects, remedies) with a defined introduction and conclusion, precise examples and a logical progression; the length 500 to 550 words is respected. |
| Expression | 8 | Formal register, varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary (rigging, ballot stuffing, legitimacy, impunity), well-chosen connectors (secondly, however, in conclusion). |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation. |

**Common errors**

- Treating the title as a narrative or a political speech, or naming real parties and persons: the topic calls for a balanced, impersonal discussion.
- Listing forms of fraud without causes, effects or solutions, so that the essay is one-sided and too short.
